# Trellis For Rust Consumers

Rust-specific usage of Trellis. Read it with [the Trellis guide](llms-core.txt)
from the same Trellis revision, which covers the language-neutral model,
authorization, surfaces, and resources.

## Overview

Trellis does not prescribe an application's configuration parser, database,
domain types, DI pattern, logging setup, or test framework. Trellis's supported
Rust toolchain is current stable. Use `/api` for current Rustdoc and the
generated participant source for project-specific APIs; private Trellis
workspace crates are not consumer dependencies.

`trellis-protocol` authenticates Auth's signed records (catalog snapshots,
provider certificates, issuer rotations, logical-session authority, and
revocations) against pinned instance/account trust. Catalog membership checks
also require verified live authority and its retirement status; decoding a
record is not trust.

## Generated Package

Author native IDL and set `[package]`, `[sources]`, and `[generate.rust].output`
in `trellis.toml`. A durable `consumer` requires a direct `trellis` source
package dependency containing `trellis.events@v1`; select and lock its version
before generation.

The output is one ordinary crate at the source package version, with
`orders_trellis::apis::<api>`, `orders_trellis::participants::<participant>`, and
`orders_trellis::apps::<request>` modules, not independent SDK or participant
crates. Add an ordinary Cargo path dependency, for example
`orders-trellis = { path = "trellis" }`. The generated crate declares the
published runtime dependency matching the CLI. It has no generator build script,
repository-relative runtime paths, or runtime-path config in `trellis.toml`. Use
ordinary Cargo overrides when developing against a local runtime. Generation
does not modify the consumer's Cargo manifest.

An API SDK contains types and descriptors. The participant facade supplies the
connection boundary and only the declared caller/provider surfaces. Its
constants carry source-package/participant evidence; applications do not supply
digests to service bootstrap. Matching built-in models come from
`trellis-models` rather than being copied into each generated package;
package-name equality alone never substitutes one schema for another. A
support-ABI mismatch fails compilation and is not resolved through compatibility
wrappers.

Generated models keep wire distinctions: an optional field is `Option<T>`
(`None` when omitted), `T | null` is `Nullable<T>`, so an optional nullable
field decodes an explicit `null` as `Some(Nullable::Null)`. The IDL `json` type
is `serde_json::Value`; an optional `json` field decodes a present `null` as
`Some(Value::Null)`. Every model has an
`extra` map preserving unknown fields and every enum an `Unknown(String)`
variant; authored field `extra` or enum value `unknown` is rejected.

### Features

`trellis-rs` enables `native-oauth` (native OAuth sign-in and installation
discovery) and `device` (device enrollment and activation) by default. Services
need `native-oauth` for discovery; a service may build with
`default-features = false, features = ["native-oauth"]` to drop `device`.
`telemetry-otlp` adds the OTLP exporter. Enable
`event-store-sqlite` for `SqliteInboxStore`/`SqliteOutboxStore` or
`event-store-postgres` for `PostgresInboxStore`/`PostgresOutboxStore`;
database-specific `EventStoreError` variants follow the same features, and
neither SQL driver is enabled by default.

SDK HTTP connections and `telemetry-otlp` exporters preserve an
application-installed Rustls provider, otherwise use ring locally without
changing the process-wide provider, and verify certificates against platform
trust.

## Connection

The generated crate is named after the `[package]` name. Each participant is a
module joining package, participant, and (for APIs) major version, such as
`participants::acme_orders_orders_service`, `apps::acme_orders_orders_caller`,
and `apis::acme_orders_orders_v1`. A service module exports `Participant` and
`Provider`. Discover the installation for its broker endpoints and pinned
`RuntimeAuthorizationTrust`, then connect with the provisioned identity seed
from `trellis_rs::service::ServiceConnectOptions`. Name and timeout are
optional builders:

```rust
use acme_orders::participants::acme_orders_orders_service::{Participant, Provider};
use trellis_rs::auth::{discover_accepting_certificate, CertificateAcceptance};
use trellis_rs::service::ServiceConnectOptions;

let server = discover_accepting_certificate(
    &trellis_url,
    &CertificateAcceptance::for_program("orders-service"),
)
.await?;
let mut service = Participant::connect(
    ServiceConnectOptions::new(server.nats_servers, server.trust, &identity_seed)
        .with_name("orders-service")
        .with_timeout_ms(10_000),
)
.await?;
Provider::new(&mut service)
    .acme_orders_orders_v1()
    .register_create(|_context, input| async move { create_order(input).await });
service.run().await?;
```

The discovery call is
`discover_accepting_certificate(issuer, &CertificateAcceptance::for_program("orders-service"))`
(the Console's address works; it names the sign-in issuer). A certificate the platform trust store vouches for
needs nothing. A development installation's own certificate is accepted like a
browser would: its issuer's SHA-256 fingerprint must match
`TRELLIS_CERTIFICATE_FINGERPRINT`, or `TRELLIS_ACCEPT_SELF_SIGNED=1` accepts it
on first contact, or the operator accepts it on a terminal. The answer is
remembered per program and server, a later different certificate is refused,
and the returned trust carries it into the broker connection. A known CA file
still works through `discover_native_oauth(issuer, &[ca_path])`. Never disable
certificate verification.

When the build differs from the revision its instance runs, `connect` submits
the build and returns once it installs. A build that asks for new access waits
for an administrator, logging the review link and printing it as a QR code on
stderr; a rejection returns `ServiceRuntimeError::UpdateRejected { review }`,
naming the review link or, without a Console, the CLI command that shows it.

`service.health()` adds to the automatic heartbeats:
`set_info(ServiceHealthInfo { version, info })` (or `set_info_with` for values
computed per heartbeat) and `add(name, || async { ServiceHealthCheck::ok() })`,
whose returned registration's `remove()` drops the check. A device's connected
client has the same `health()`.

Register generated providers before `service.run().await`. The service lifecycle
supervises its request host and workers. `with_timeout_ms(...)` bounds
bootstrap, connect, and request operations. No context-store parameter exists.
Retain generated facades, still-bound resources, and job references across
transport handoffs.

### Native applications

Apps and agents acquire native OAuth admission through the selected
authorization origin. Pass the verified `NativeOAuthSession` and explicit broker
endpoints to `UserConnectOptions::new(nats_servers, timeout_ms, session)`. Use
Authorization Code with PKCE or Device Code according to the registered native
client's flow. For Device Code, show `verification_uri_complete()` (the link
with the code filled in; fall back to `verification_uri()`) and `user_code()`
for comparison. Do not persist a bare session seed as a substitute for OAuth
custody. The SDK retains credential custody and renews admission with the same
runtime identity and key, using its owner's authenticated issuer pin. Recovery
failure closes application transport without deleting the durable credential
record.

Native OAuth custody binds each credential handle to the selected issuer,
installation, NATS account, and client identity. Owner-only files retain the
persistent DPoP key and rotating refresh family; an operating-system lock spans
read, exchange, and commit across processes. Recovery is marked before exchange
so a lost response cannot trigger replay of a spent refresh token. Platforms
without the owner-only adapter must supply an explicit secure-store adapter. The
native CLI uses the same custody.

Native OAuth renewal leases the current maintenance transport after HTTP
refresh and retains it through signer lookup and verified authority promotion;
replacing the physical NATS generation does not pin renewal to the original
socket. Explicit native authority refresh uses the scheduled renewal worker and
awaits authenticated publication and coverage.

### Devices

Devices retain their provisioned identity seed and use generated activation and
connect options. `DeviceActivationOptions` proves durable and ephemeral key
possession for the one-use enrollment secret. For a companion, declare Auth's
`deviceCompanionsManage` capability in the child request, obtain ordinary
explicit native OAuth consent, associate with `DeviceCompanions.Attach` from
that verified user connection, then drop the setup client and resume the same
credential handle. Supply its independent `UserConnectOptions` via
`DeviceConnectOptions::with_companion`; signed assignment must match the
descriptor, native client, and exact OAuth grant.

## Typed Surfaces

Use the participant's generated methods. Each used API is an accessor named
like its `apis` module, with one method per RPC: an app or agent calls
`client.acme_orders_orders_v1().create(&input)`, a device calls the same
accessor on its connected `Client`, and a service calls through
`Provider::new(&mut service).client()`. A service registers what it implements
through `Provider::new(&mut service).acme_orders_orders_v1().register_create(...)`.
Argument and result types come from the generated crate; every model carries an
`extra` map (`extra: Default::default()` when constructing one).

Exact method and model names come from the generated crate. Match generated
declared-error variants directly; transport and unknown remote failures remain
distinct. Native no-responder replies become `ServiceUnavailableError`, exposed
through `CallError::ServiceUnavailable` or
`TrellisClientError::ServiceUnavailable`. Generated cursor-paginated RPCs add
lazy fallible page/item streams; a missing `next_cursor` is the sole end signal.

A handler reports a failure with no declared error as
`ServerError::Internal(message)`. The text goes only to the service's log.
Callers receive `UnexpectedError` with a fixed message, its `id`, `traceId` and
`context.requestId`, and the log line carries the same IDs. A failed Operation
carries `id` and `traceId`, and its log line also has the operation ID.

Rust schema-validation issue paths use JSON Pointer: an empty path is the root,
`/` is an empty-name property, and property names escape `~` as `~0` and `/` as
`~1`, including missing required fields.

### Events

Owned event publication uses generated publishers. Durable handlers use declared
Consumer resources; Trellis resolves durable identity, local concurrency, retry,
authority, and scoped Events DLQ/replay. Invalid core NATS publications are
dropped without ending a healthy stream. Retain the returned listener guard:
dropping or aborting it removes that registration without stopping the others
in its group. Shared pull-loop failures are reported by the service lifecycle,
and unmatched messages are not acknowledged as completed work.

### Operations

Operations expose generated invokers and typed references for start, wait,
progress/watch, and optional cancellation/transfer. Persist a caller-selected
ULID before `start_with_invocation_id(id, &input)`; this is the durable
operation ID. `OperationRef::reference()` exposes the complete serializable
owner reference; restore it with the invoker's `control(reference)` without
starting another execution. To cancel a reserved invocation that may not yet be
admitted, use `start_cancelled_with_invocation_id(id, &input)` with its original
input; the returned reference does not imply finished cleanup, so `wait()` for
the terminal result.

For explicit pre-acceptance owner selection, persist deployment, invocation
ULID, and frozen input before sending, then use
`start_on_deployment_with_invocation_id(deployment_id, invocation_id, &input)`
or `start_cancelled_on_deployment_with_invocation_id(deployment_id,
invocation_id, &input)`.

In a handler, `control.operation_ref()` is the operation's complete serialized
reference; a caller restores it with the generated operation's `control(ref)`.

A handler that hands its work elsewhere, such as to a job, calls
`control.defer()` and returns `Ok(())`: the instance keeps the operation's lease
until it ends. Returning `Ok(())` without a terminal state and without deferring
lets the lease lapse, and recovery runs the handler again. `register_<op>`
returns an `OperationRegistration`. Its `control(id)` returns the owner-fenced
`OperationControl` of an execution this instance runs, including a deferred one,
so other code can report progress or `complete`/`fail` it; any other instance
gets `ServerError::OperationNotFound`. `reconcile(id)` asks the current owner,
on any replica, to enter the handler again with the stored input and returns the
snapshot once that entry returns; it never takes over a live lease.

Operation handlers can clone `control.cancellation()` and observe `Requested`,
`OwnershipLost`, or `ServiceStopping` with `is_cancelled()`, `reason()`, or
`cancelled().await`. They must stop and join owned child work, including
already-running `spawn_blocking` closures, before returning from requested
cancellation. A cleanup handler error leaves cancellation nonterminal for
recovery. Recovered handlers enter with `Requested` already set and must retry
cleanup without starting new business work; return `Ok(())` only after cleanup
succeeds. External effects may still overlap across owner loss; use idempotency
or external fencing.

### Jobs

Jobs are private service queues. Use generated queue handles and cloneable
`jobs_client()` handles for submission from other handlers. `create_<job>`
returns a `JobRef` (a refused keyed job is `JobsError::NotEnqueued`);
`submit_<job>` returns the `JobSubmitOutcome`. Handlers report durable
`progress`/`log`, wrap outside waits in `wait_for(edge, future)`, and for a queue
declaring `update` publish live-only updates with `job.emit_update(update)`.
Subscribe with `job_ref.updates()` or `provider.<job>_updates(&id)`: a validated,
ordered stream that ends at the job's terminal state and never replays earlier
updates. Forward them through an operation's `emit_update` to reach callers. Worker registration
and processing are supervised by the service lifecycle, and delivery progress
acknowledgement is automatic. Before business work, inspect
`job.cancellation_token().reason()`: already-cancelled job handlers must
reconcile earlier side effects. A recovered owner after fail-stale takeover sees
`JobCancellationReason::StaleAttempt`.

## Resources

Use generated State, KV, Store, Consumer, and Job handles. Resolved binding
payloads and subjects are runtime internals.

App State accessors register generated native-IDL schemas asynchronously:
`let (state, registration) = client.saved_resource("0", idempotency_key).await?;`
(accepted historical versions add `&Migrations`).
`let mut observation = state.watch().await?;` uses certified Live Watch, and
`observation.next().await` returns
`Option<Result<Option<StateValue<T>>, StateReadError>>`: outer None ends
observation, inner None means unwritten or deleted. Use
`observation.close().await?` and `observation.closed().await`; drop also closes.

`StoreResourceHandle::list_page` and file metadata listing use the shared keyset
pagination. Store readers and writers support bounded streaming through
`write_from` and `read_into`. Reader drop starts owned cleanup on the creating
Tokio runtime, including cross-thread drops; cleanup retains the generation
lease. Whole-buffer helpers consume the same reader but retain the entire
object in memory.

### Transfers

Generated Operation references upload bytes with `upload(body)` or stream with
`upload_from(reader)`; lower-level operation builders stream with
`transfer_from(reader)` without a caller-supplied size or hash. Trellis counts
and hashes bytes while sending and verifies size and SHA-256 on receipt.
Download destination writes and upload backend-reader consumption release
credit. Backend uploads pipeline bounded writes but await required
acknowledgements and metadata commit before success. Cancellation before commit
aborts staging; after commit it cannot undo the committed object. Cancel an
upload with `upload_from_with_cancel(reader, &TransferCancellation)`: it returns
`TransferCancelled` once the provider confirms, or `Timeout` after the client
timeout when it does not, with remote cleanup unconfirmed.

A `stream;` Operation handler takes the caller's live bytes with
`operation.take_upload_stream()` (an `AsyncRead`, returned once). End of file
means verified size/digest and recorded delivery, after which
`operation.upload()` returns the metadata; a failed transfer is a read error.
Serve generated downloads with
`context.plan_stream_download_transfer(id, expires_at, info)` and
`context.handle().spawn_stream_download_endpoint(plan, reader)`; `info` declares
the exact size and digest.

### Transactional events

Prepared events and jobs let outbox intents participate in a local SQL
transaction. Store `prepare_event::<Descriptor>(...)` or the generated
`jobs.prepare_<job>(payload)` with `store.enqueue(id, &intent)`; the job's ID is
fixed at preparation. `dispatch_outbox_once(&mut store,
&jobs.outbox_dispatcher())` claims one intent and publishes the event or
submits the job, returning `Published` or `JobDispatched` with the queue's
`OutboxJobOutcome`. A key policy's refusal is final and records the job as
skipped; only dispatcher errors retry. A repeated job dispatch does not create a
second job. Pass the claimed record to `mark_published`/`mark_failed`; false
means ownership was superseded, and `dispatch_outbox_once` returns `ClaimLost`
for superseded completion. SQL tables have a `kind` column (`event` or `job`).
The application owns its transaction and migration execution. See current
Rustdoc for supported stores.

## Accounts

Generated account calls follow the language-neutral rules. Use
`user.account.profile_revision` as `expected_revision` for
`users_profile_update` with an idempotency key. Administrative `users_update`
uses lifecycle `expected_revision`; omit unchanged profile fields for
lifecycle-only saves, and add `expected_profile_revision` for intentional
profile edits. Both revisions are checked atomically. Directory `avatar_url`
follows the shared avatar rules.

## Test And Verify

Run generation and the consuming project's own Cargo checks. A Rust test uses
the published `trellis-testkit` crate, which owns production server and broker
processes, chooses loopback ports automatically, and returns the existing SDK
connection options so generated service and app facades connect normally. No
source checkout or compiler/runtime Cargo dependencies are required. The bare
builder downloads the latest Trellis CLI/server release (or
`TRELLIS_TEST_VERSION`), verified against its published checksum, and a pinned
NATS archive (network on first use); the verified cache
(`TRELLIS_TEST_CACHE_DIR`, otherwise the platform cache) lets later runtimes
boot offline. Set `TRELLIS_TEST_NATS_BIN`, choose `NatsSource::Path`, or choose
`NatsSource::PathLookup` for a prebuilt broker. Set `TRELLIS_TEST_SERVER_BIN`, or use `NativeSource::Path { server }`, for
explicit binaries with no fallback downloads. `trust_roots()` and
`https_client_builder()` trust the runtime's generated CA. `restart()` restarts
only the server, retaining its broker and durable installation;
shutdown/cancellation reaps owned children before sandbox cleanup.

Live user tests use `TrellisTestRuntime::create_user`, explicit
`grant_user_capabilities(&user, Request::REQUIRED_CAPABILITIES)`, one
`register_native_application::<Request>("app")`, then independent
`login_native_application_as(&app, &user)` calls. `register_client_as` composes
registration and login, and `register_client` retains its seeded-administrator
convenience.

A real-runtime test can also launch a Rust service from a Node test using
`@oatscenter/trellis-testkit`; see the TypeScript guide.
